opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Amara. I'm a researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group that studies how people see changes at work, and nothing you tell me will be linked to your name.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Happy to. This is basically what I argue about at dinner, so I'm glad someone's asking properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a great tool. Our wind and solar forecasts are better because of it, and that keeps the grid cleaner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, this version is great for me. I build these models. If it stays a tool, I'm one of the people who knows best how to use it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep building. Push for better forecasting in our team. Maybe run a short course for colleagues.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Happy. Like a good day at work.

S0.say: It's a great tool. Our wind and solar forecasts are better because of it.
S0.think: This version is great for me. I'm one of the people who knows best how to use it.
S0.do: Keeps building, pushes for better forecasting and runs a short course for colleagues.
S0.feel: Happy, like a good day at work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say slow change is a chance to get the rules right, about who owns the tools and who benefits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, fine. My worry is junior hiring. Fewer beginners now means fewer experienced people later, and fewer people from outside the usual circles getting in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mentor a couple of juniors on purpose. Keep building.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit restless about the ladder.

S1.say: Slow change is a chance to get the rules right about who owns the tools and who benefits.
S1.think: Fine for me. Fewer beginners means fewer people from outside the usual circles getting in.
S1.do: Mentors a couple of juniors on purpose and keeps building.
S1.feel: Calm, a bit restless about the ladder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the gains from these tools are going to a few companies and their shareholders. We need strong unions, retraining and a fair tax on those profits. I'd write about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm probably one of the people who gains. My skills get more valuable when everyone wants agents built. That doesn't sit right with me, given what's happening to everyone else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ask for a raise, honestly, because I'd get it. Give time to a group that teaches data skills to laid-off workers. Back candidates who want to tax the windfall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good for me. Uneasy about everyone else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd ask for a raise and campaign to tax the windfall. Do those sit together for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not neatly. But refusing a raise doesn't help anyone. Changing the rules does.

S2.say: The gains are going to a few companies. We need strong unions, retraining and a fair tax on those profits.
S2.think: I'm probably one of the people who gains, and that doesn't sit right with me.
S2.do: Asks for a raise, volunteers teaching data skills to laid-off workers, and backs candidates who want to tax the windfall.
S2.feel: Good for her, uneasy about everyone else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment to decide who owns the future. If share prices boom while millions lose work, that's a policy choice, and we can choose differently.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Even I'm not safe in this one. If AI matches skilled professionals, it can build forecasting models too. I'd likely be among the last to go, because I build the systems, but my team would shrink. And my family would be fine. That bothers me most, that people like us would be fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Get more involved in politics than I've ever been. Move our savings into something less tied to the AI boom, since it looks like a bubble. Keep my skills right at the edge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. More about the country than about us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said it bothers you that people like you would be fine. Would you give up some of that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. I'd vote to be taxed more, and I'd mean it.

S3.say: If share prices boom while millions lose work, that's a policy choice, and we can choose differently.
S3.think: I'd likely be among the last to go, but my team would shrink. What bothers me is that people like us would be fine.
S3.do: Gets more involved in politics than ever, moves savings away from the AI boom and keeps her skills at the edge.
S3.feel: Anxious, more about the country than her family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as before, but louder. Robots make this everyone's problem, not just office workers'.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Robots don't change my job. They change everyone else's. My neighbours, the people who look after my kid. The gap between who owns this and who doesn't gets huge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Organise. Help start or fund a local group that helps people into new work. Give more to food banks. Keep pushing for a fair tax on AI and robot profits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious and angry. Being safe myself makes it worse.

S4.say: Robots make this everyone's problem, not just office workers'.
S4.think: Robots don't change my job, they change everyone else's. The gap between owners and everyone else gets huge.
S4.do: Helps start or fund a local group that helps people into new work, gives more to food banks and pushes for a tax on AI and robot profits.
S4.feel: Anxious and angry. Being safe makes it worse.
